questions.question: Which of the following does NOT affect blood alcohol content (BAC)?

options.text: How fast the alcohol is consumed
How often the drinker consumes alcohol

questions.correctAnswerText: How often the drinker consumes alcohol
questions.explanation: Three main factors affect BAC: the amount of alcohol consumed, how fast it is consumed, and the drinker's body weight. Driving under the influence of alcohol is illegal and dangerous.

questions.question: What is the minimum following distance you should usually maintain?
questions.correctAnswerText: Two seconds
questions.explanation: Keep a minimum following distance of two seconds. In bad weather or poor conditions, increase it to at least three seconds.

questions.question: When preparing to pass another rider on the left, you should:

options.text: Move to the right part of the lane so they can see you in their side mirror.
Move to the left part of the lane to see better ahead.
Stay in the center of the lane so they can see you in their rearview mirror.
Weave in your lane to get their attention.

questions.correctAnswerText: Move to the left part of the lane to see better ahead.
questions.explanation: Ride in the left part of your lane to see better and be more visible to other drivers. Check your mirrors and look over your shoulder before changing lanes.

questions.question: If a dog is chasing your motorcycle, you should:

options.text: Stop until the dog loses interest.

questions.correctAnswerText: Slow down, then speed up.
questions.explanation: Slow down and approach the dog calmly. Then accelerate and leave it behind. If a larger animal is in your path, brake and be ready to stop.

questions.question: When riding at night, you should:

options.text: Use the headlights of the vehicle ahead to help you see.

questions.correctAnswerText: Use the headlights of the vehicle ahead to help you see.
questions.explanation: To stay safe at night, reduce your speed and increase your following distance. Use the headlights of vehicles ahead to see farther down the road. Adjust your lane position as needed.

questions.question: When riding a motorcycle, you should:

options.text: Always stay in the same part of the lane.
Change your lane position based on road and traffic conditions.
Only ride in the center of the lane so others see you.
Ride in a zigzag pattern so drivers notice you.

questions.correctAnswerText: Change your lane position based on road and traffic conditions.
questions.explanation: There is no single best lane position. Change your position as needed based on road and traffic conditions.

questions.question: When following a car, the best part of the lane to ride in is usually:
questions.correctAnswerText: The center portion.
questions.explanation: Ride in the center of the lane so the driver can see you in their rearview mirror. Drivers check their rearview mirrors more often than side mirrors, so this position keeps you more visible.

questions.question: The center of a lane often has an oily strip from cars. This strip:

options.text: Is usually safe unless the road is wet.

questions.correctAnswerText: Is usually safe unless the road is wet.
questions.explanation: Oil from cars collects in the center of lanes. When the road is dry, this area usually provides enough grip for motorcycles. The strip is usually narrow, so you can often ride beside it while still staying in the center part of the lane.

questions.question: Shatterproof goggles, a face shield, or a windshield:

options.text: Must be used when riding faster than 35 mph.
Must be used all the time.
Are only required for riders under 21.

questions.correctAnswerText: Must be used when riding faster than 35 mph.
questions.explanation: If your motorcycle has no windshield, you must wear shatterproof goggles, eyeglasses, or a face shield when riding above 35 mph to protect your eyes from road debris.

questions.question: When riding in a group, you should:

options.text: Put inexperienced riders at the back.
Not ride too close to other riders in the group.

questions.correctAnswerText: Not ride too close to other riders in the group.
questions.explanation: Use a staggered formation when riding in a group. Check your mirrors to watch riders behind you. The lead and sweep riders should be experienced. Maintain proper space between all riders.

questions.question: When another vehicle passes you from behind, what should you do?

options.text: Use the left part of your lane.
Use the center part of your lane.
Use the right part of your lane.

questions.correctAnswerText: Use the center part of your lane.
questions.explanation: The center part of your lane is the safest position when being passed. Riding on the side closest to the passing vehicle risks a collision. Riding on the far side may make the other driver return to your lane too soon.

questions.question: What does this hand signal mean?

options.text: I am about to slow down.

questions.correctAnswerText: I am turning right.
questions.explanation: Instead of using turn signals, you can use hand signals. When the left arm is bent at the elbow and pointing upward, it means you plan to turn right or change lanes to the right.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a benefit of a proper lane position?

options.text: It helps you set up for turns.
It gives you an escape route.
It helps you avoid wind blasts from other vehicles.
It places you in another vehicle's blind spot.

questions.correctAnswerText: It places you in another vehicle's blind spot.
questions.explanation: A good lane position should help you see others and be seen. It should help you avoid wind blasts, blind spots, and road hazards. Your position should prevent other vehicles from sharing your lane and give you a way to escape if danger appears.

questions.question: What does this hand signal mean?
questions.correctAnswerText: Turn right
questions.explanation: You can use hand signals instead of or along with turn signals. When your left arm is bent at the elbow and pointing upward, it means you plan to turn right or change lanes to the right.

questions.question: When carrying a heavy load, what should you adjust?
questions.correctAnswerText: The suspension.
questions.explanation: Before riding with a heavy load, adjust your tire pressure, spring pre-load, air shocks, and dampers to the settings for that weight.

questions.question: If road conditions make stopping harder, what should you do?

options.text: Stay closer to the vehicle ahead.
Stay farther from the vehicle ahead.
Let someone else ride your motorcycle.

questions.correctAnswerText: Stay farther from the vehicle ahead.
questions.explanation: You need more space behind other vehicles when stopping takes longer. On slippery pavement, if you cannot see through the vehicle ahead, or if traffic is heavy, maintain at least a three-second following distance.

questions.question: What following distance should you normally keep?
questions.correctAnswerText: Two seconds
questions.explanation: In normal conditions, keep at least two seconds between you and the vehicle ahead. Increase this distance when conditions are poor.

questions.question: When you are about to pass a vehicle on the left, where should you ride in your lane?

options.text: The left part of the lane
The center part of the lane
The right part of the lane

questions.correctAnswerText: The left part of the lane
questions.explanation: Ride in the left part of your lane when passing another vehicle. This helps you see ahead better and makes you more visible to oncoming traffic.

questions.question: If your rear tire locks up, how do you regain control?
questions.correctAnswerText: Release the rear brake.
questions.explanation: To regain control of a locked rear wheel, release the brake. However, if the rear brake locks on good pavement, you can keep it locked until the motorcycle stops.

questions.question: If you carry a load in a sidecar, how does it affect stopping distance?

options.text: It is the same as a regular motorcycle.

questions.correctAnswerText: It may increase stopping distance.
questions.explanation: A heavier motorcycle takes longer to stop because it has more weight. Start slowing down and stopping earlier when riding a motorcycle with a load or passenger in the sidecar.
